verses.text: It was now just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knew that His hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father. Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end.
The evening meal was underway, and the devil had already put into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray Jesus.
Jesus knew that the Father had delivered all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was returning to God.
So He got up from the supper, laid aside His outer garments, and wrapped a towel around His waist.
After that, He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and dry them with the towel that was around Him.
He came to Simon Peter, who asked Him, "Lord, are You going to wash my feet?"
Jesus replied, "You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand."
"Never shall You wash my feet!" Peter told Him. Jesus answered, "Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me."
"Then, Lord," Simon Peter replied, "not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!"
Jesus told him, "Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he will be completely clean. And you are clean, though not all of you."
For He knew who would betray Him. That is why He said, "Not all of you are clean."
When Jesus had washed their feet and put on His outer garments, He reclined with them again and asked, "Do you know what I have done for you?
You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am.
So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another's feet.
I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you.
Truly, truly, I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.
If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.
I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is to fulfill the Scripture: 'The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.'
I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever receives the one I send receives Me, and whoever receives Me receives the One who sent Me."
After Jesus had said this, He became troubled in spirit and testified, "Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will betray Me."
The disciples looked at one another, perplexed as to which of them He meant.
One of His disciples, the one whom Jesus loved, was reclining at His side.
So Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus which one He was talking about.
Leaning back against Jesus, he asked, "Lord, who is it?"
Jesus answered, "It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it." Then He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot.
And when Judas had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to Judas, "What you are about to do, do quickly."
But no one at the table knew why Jesus had said this to him.
Since Judas kept the money bag, some thought that Jesus was telling him to buy what was needed for the feast, or to give something to the poor.
As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night.
When Judas had gone out, Jesus said, "Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him.
If God is glorified in Him, God will also glorify the Son in Himself—and will glorify Him at once.
Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for Me, and as I said to the Jews, so now I say to you: 'Where I am going, you cannot come.'
A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another."
"Lord, where are You going?" Simon Peter asked. Jesus answered, "Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later."
"Lord," said Peter, "why can't I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You."
"Will you lay down your life for Me?" Jesus replied. "Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times."

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Theological narrative — the opening of John's extended farewell section (chapters 13-17), Jesus' private teaching to His disciples alone on the night before His death
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: Early Christian tradition locates this upper room on Mount Zion in Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations nearby have uncovered first-century ritual purification baths, underscoring just how seriously purity customs were taken at Passover — making Jesus' choice to personally wash dusty feet, rather than insist on formal ritual washing, all the more pointed.
context.custom: Washing a guest's feet was standard hospitality in a world of sandals and dusty roads, but it was specifically the lowest household task, normally assigned to the least-senior servant present — often a Gentile or female slave, never expected of a guest's own social equals, let alone their acknowledged teacher.
context.timelineImmediate: This chapter opens John's long farewell discourse, occupying the entire night before Jesus' arrest — the footwashing, Judas's departure into the literal and symbolic darkness, and Jesus' new commandment all happen in a single continuous evening, with everything from chapter 14 onward still part of that same night's conversation.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' words "the one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me" quote Psalm 41:9 directly — David's own betrayal by a trusted friend now finding its fuller, final fulfillment in Judas's betrayal of Jesus at this very meal.
context.sparkNotes: On the night before His death, Jesus performs the lowest household task available — washing His disciples' feet — turning it into a living lesson in humble service just before identifying His betrayer by handing him bread at the same table. Once Judas slips out into the night, Jesus gives what He calls a new commandment: to love one another exactly as He has loved them, a mark meant to identify His followers to the watching world. The chapter closes with Peter's confident vow of loyalty, met immediately by Jesus' precise prediction of his coming triple denial.

translation.meaning: Specifically refers to washing a part of the body (as opposed to full bathing) — a word for an everyday, lowly household task, not a ceremonial or symbolic act in its ordinary usage.

Not new in the sense that loving one's neighbor was never commanded before, but new in its standard — love measured against Jesus' own self-giving love, a fresh and much higher bar than anything commanded previously.
Literally "to hand over" or "deliver up" — the same word used throughout the Passion narrative for handing Jesus over to His accusers, giving Judas's specific betrayal a grim, almost legal precision.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parallel account of Jesus identifying His betrayer at the table.
Mark's version of the same identification of Judas.
Luke's parallel account of Jesus predicting Peter's denial.

otBackground.note: "He who shares my bread has lifted up his heel against me" — quoted directly by Jesus to describe His own betrayal by Judas.
The suffering servant's exaltation despite disfigurement and rejection — background for Jesus' repeated language of being "glorified" even as His betrayal unfolds.
"Love your neighbor as yourself" — the older commandment Jesus' "new commandment" deliberately raises to a new, self-sacrificial standard.

mapCoords.placeName: The Upper Room, Mount Zion, Jerusalem

commentary.note: Henry notes the Greek phrase behind 'loved them to the end' is eis telos — literally 'to perfection' — reading Jesus' love as constant and complete rather than merely lasting until a deadline: 'nothing can separate a believer from the love of Christ; he loves his own... unto perfection.'

On why loving one another counts as a 'new' commandment when Leviticus already required it, Henry explains that rabbinic tradition had buried the original command under layers of permitted revenge and self-interest — 'as it came from Christ new, it was new to the people,' restored rather than invented, but genuinely new in the form they'd actually receive it.

A modern commentary observes something easy to miss: Jesus washes the feet of every disciple at that table without exception — including 'the feet of the one who will betray him before the meal is even over, Judas... and the one who will deny being one of his disciples, Peter.' The act of love comes before either failure, not after repentance.
